keyVerseText: These be the names of the mighty men whom David had: The Tachmonite that sat in the seat , chief among the captains; the same was Adino the Eznite: he lift up his spear against eight hundred, whom he slew at one time. The Tachmonite: or, Joshebbassebet the Tachmonite, head of the three. whom he: Heb. slain. he lift: See 1.Ch.11.11. whom he: Heb. slain
rootMeaning: The root of תַּחְכְּמֹנִי (Tachkᵉmônîy) is likely חַכְמוֹנִי (Chakmôwnîy), which carries the meaning of 'wise' or 'sagacious.' This etymology suggests that the name conveys a sense of wisdom or prudence, going beyond a mere tribal or geographic designation to imply a characteristic of insightfulness or understanding. The literal sense 'thou will make me wise' enriches the English gloss by highlighting a personal or familial identity connected to wisdom.
usageInScripture: This term appears only once in Scripture, specifically in 2 Samuel 23:8, where it serves as a descriptive designation for Josheb-basshebeth, one of David's mighty warriors. The consistent translation as 'The Tachmonite' underscores its function as an ethnic or clan identifier, linking the individual to a particular lineage known for wisdom. The singular occurrence emphasizes its specificity and importance in identifying a notable figure within David's elite forces.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding תַּחְכְּמֹנִי as rooted in wisdom invites reflection on the biblical value of wisdom as a divine gift and a mark of godly leadership. The association of this term with one of David's chief warriors highlights how wisdom and strength coexist in those who serve God's purposes. For the Christian faith, it underscores that spiritual wisdom is foundational for faithful service and leadership in God's kingdom. This name reminds believers that true might is accompanied by insight granted from God, aligning with the biblical theme that wisdom is more valuable than mere power.
keyVerseReflection: In 2 Samuel 23:8, 'The Tachmonite' is identified as a chief among David's captains, specifically Josheb-basshebeth, who demonstrated remarkable valor by slaying eight hundred men at once. The use of תַּחְכְּמֹנִי here not only situates him ethnically but also subtly conveys that his prowess was coupled with wisdom or strategic insight. This enriches the portrait of David's mighty men, showing that their strength was not only physical but also marked by discernment and divine enablement.
